description: We’re GeoSleuth, a team from Kosovo working on “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” We’re building a web app that turns decades of NASA data into clear answers: what’s changing where you live, how fast, and when the change became undeniable. You can even listen to each trend as sound. Our skills: Python, data, statistics, machine learning and AI agents. We’d welcome a designer or someone with an Earth or climate science background. Message us!
summary:
GeoSleuth is a web app that answers a simple question: is the climate where you live really changing, and how sure can we be? Users pick any place on Earth, and GeoSleuth analyzes 24 years (2001-2024) of NASA POWER data across eight climate variables, including temperature, extremes, rainfall, humidity, soil moisture and sunlight. For each one, it gives an honest verdict: emerged, emerging, or no clear signal.

To address the Trend Detective challenge, GeoSleuth separates real trends from natural year-to-year noise using methods climate scientists use: Sen's slope, the Mann-Kendall test with pre-whitening, a signal-to-noise emergence test, false discovery control across variables, and robustness checks with shifted start years. We validated NASA POWER rainfall against NASA GPM IMERG satellite data (correlation 0.90, same verdict). Users can investigate one trend, compare two places, explore case files, and even listen to a trend as sound.

This matters because people often mistake a few unusual years for climate change, or dismiss real change as noise. GeoSleuth makes trustworthy climate evidence accessible to anyone.
details:
GeoSleuth tells you if the climate where you live is really changing, and how sure we can be. Pick any place on Earth and it analyzes 24 years (2001-2024) of NASA POWER data across up to nine climate variables, such as temperature, extremes, rainfall, soil moisture and sunlight.

For each variable, it removes the seasonal cycle, measures the trend with Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test, and labels it Emerged (the change is clearly bigger than natural noise), Emerging, or No clear signal. False discovery control and robustness checks keep it from raising false alarms. We validated NASA POWER rainfall against NASA GPM IMERG satellite data (correlation 0.90, same verdict).

Users can scan a place, investigate one trend, compare two places, open case files, and even listen to a trend as sound, with a written description for accessibility.

Impact: anyone can get an honest, evidence-based answer about climate change in their own place.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, Plotly, Folium, SciPy, pymannkendall, NASA POWER API, NASA Giovanni, OpenStreetMap. Code is open source on GitHub.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
